{{Short description|Bound on the coefficients of a factor polynomial}}
In [[algebra]], a '''Landau–Mignotte bound''' (sometimes only referred to as '''Mignotte's bound'''<ref name=mathWorld>{{cite web |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Landau-MignotteBound.html |title=Landau–Mignotte Bound |last=Bhatt |first=Bhuvanesh |website=MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource, created by Eric W. Weisstein |publisher=Wolfram Research Inc. |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref>) is one of a family of inequalities concerning a [[univariate polynomial|univariate]] [[integer polynomial]] ''f''(''x'') and one of its factors ''h''(''x''). A basic version states that the [[coefficient]]s of ''h''(''x'') are bounded independently of ''h''(''x'') by an [[exponential function|exponential expression]] involving only the [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] and coefficients of ''f''(''x''), i.e. only depending on ''f''(''x'').

It has applications in [[computer algebra]] where these bounds can give a priori estimates on the run time and [[computational complexity|complexity]] of [[algorithm]]s.<ref name=vzG>{{cite book |last1=von zur Gathen |first1=Joachim |last2=Gerhard |first2=Jürgen |date=2013 |title=Modern Computer Algebra |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/modern-computer-algebra/DB3563D4013401734851CF683D2F03F0 |location=Cambridge UK |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781139856065}}</ref>

==Basic version==

For <math>f(x),h(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]</math> such that <math>h(x)</math> [[Divisibility (ring theory)|divides]] <math>f(x)</math> denote by <math>\|h\|_{1}</math> resp. <math>\|f\|_{1}</math> the sum of the [[absolute value]]s of the [[coefficient]]s of <math>h(x)</math> resp. <math>f(x)</math> and let <math>n</math> be the degree of <math>f(x)</math>, then
:<math>\|h\|_{1}\leq 2^{n}\|f\|_{1}</math>

==Notation==

<math>f,g,h\in\mathbb{C}[x]</math> will be univariate [[complex polynomial]]s which later will be restricted to be [[integer polynomial]]s, i.e. in <math>\mathbb{Z}[x]</math>. Explicitly
:<math>
f=\sum\limits_{i=0}^nf_ix^i,\ \ \ 
g=\sum\limits_{i=0}^mg_ix^i,\ \ \ 
h=\sum\limits_{i=0}^kh_ix^i.
</math>
<math>n,m,k</math> are the [[degree of a polynomial|degrees]], the leading coefficients are <math>f_n,g_m,h_k</math>.

Define [[Norm (mathematics)|norms]] by considering the coefficients as vectors, explicitly
:<math>
\|f\|_{\infty}=\max_{0\leq i\leq n}|f_i|,\ \ \ 
\|f\|_{2}=\left(\sum\limits_{i=0}^n|f_i|^2\right)^{1/2},\ \ \ 
\|f\|_{1}=\sum\limits_{i=0}^n|f_i|.
</math>
By the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]] <math>f</math> has <math>n</math> roots <math>z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n</math> (with [[Multiplicity (mathematics)|multiplicity]]). Set the [[Mahler measure]] of <math>f</math> to be
:<math>M(f)=|f_n|\prod\limits_{i=1}^n\max\{1,|z_i|\}.</math>
Similarly define <math>\|g\|_{2}</math>, <math>M(h)</math>, etc.

==Landau's inequality and other basic properties==

[[Edmund Landau|Landau]] proved<ref name=Landau>{{cite journal |last=Landau |first=Edmund  |date=1905 |title=Sur quelques théorèmes de M. Petrovitch relatifs aux zéros des fonctions analytiques |journal=
Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France |volume=33 |pages=251–261 |doi=10.24033/BSMF.760|doi-access=free }}</ref> in 1905 a key [[Geometrical properties of polynomial roots#Landau's inequality|inequality]] linking the Mahler measure of a polynomial to its [[Norm (mathematics)#Euclidean norm|Euclidean norm]].
:<math>M(f)\leq\|f\|_{2}</math>

In general [[Norm (mathematics)#Equivalence|norms obey the following inequalities]]
:<math>\|f\|_{\infty}\leq\|f\|_{2}\leq\|f\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{n+1}\|f\|_{2}\leq(n+1)\|f\|_{\infty}.</math>

The Mahler measure satisfies <math>M(f)\geq|f_n|</math> which for non-trivial integer polynomials implies <math>M(f)\geq 1</math>. See also [[Lehmer's conjecture]].

The Mahler measure is multiplicative, i.e. if <math>f=gh</math> then
:<math>M(f)=M(g)M(h).</math>

==Mignotte's bound==

Mignotte used Landau's inequality in 1974 to prove a basic version<ref name=Mignotte>{{cite journal |last=Mignotte |first=Maurice |date=1974 |title=An Inequality About Factors of Polynomials |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=28 |issue=128 |pages=1153–1157 |doi=10.2307/2005373 |jstor=2005373 |doi-access=free }}</ref> of the following bounds{{r|vzG|pp=164 ff}} in the notation introduced above.

'''For complex polynomials''' in <math>\mathbb{C}[x]</math>, if <math>h</math> divides <math>f</math> then
:<math>
\|h\|_{1} \leq
2^{k}M(h) \leq 
2^k\frac{|h_k|}{|f_n|}\|f\|_2 \leq 
2^n\frac{|h_k|}{|f_n|}\|f\|_2
</math>
and individual coefficients obey the inequalities
:<math>
|h_i| \leq
\binom{k}{i}M(h) \leq 
\binom{k}{i}\frac{|h_k|}{|f_n|}\|f\|_2 \leq 
\binom{n}{i}\frac{|h_k|}{|f_n|}\|f\|_2
</math>

If additionally <math>f</math> and <math>h</math> are '''integer polynomials''' in <math>\mathbb{Z}[x]</math> then <math>0<\frac{|h_k|}{|f_n|}\leq 1</math> and if <math>f</math> is additionally [[Monic polynomial|monic]] then even <math>\frac{|h_k|}{|f_n|}=1</math>. In these cases one can simplify by omitting the fraction. Including products in the analysis we have the following theorem.

Let <math>f,g,h\in\mathbb{Z}[x]</math> such that <math>gh</math> divides <math>f</math> then
:<math>
\|g\|_{\infty}\|h\|_{\infty} \leq
\|g\|_{2}\|h\|_{2} \leq
\|g\|_{1}\|h\|_{1} \leq
2^{m+k}\|f\|_2 \leq 
2^{n}\sqrt{n+1}\|f\|_{\infty},
</math>
:<math>
\|h\|_{\infty} \leq
\|h\|_{2} \leq
\|h\|_{1} \leq
2^{k}\|f\|_2 \leq 
2^n\|f\|_2 \leq 
2^n\|f\|_1,
</math>
:<math>
\|h\|_{\infty} \leq
\|h\|_{2} \leq
\|h\|_{1} \leq
2^{k}\|f\|_2 \leq 
2^{k}\sqrt{n+1}\|f\|_{\infty} \leq 
2^{n}\sqrt{n+1}\|f\|_{\infty},
</math>
:<math>
|h_i| \leq
\binom{k}{i}M(h) \leq 
\binom{k}{i}\|f\|_2 \leq 
\binom{n}{i}\|f\|_2,
</math>
:<math>
\|h\|_{\infty} \leq 
\binom{k}{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\|f\|_2 \leq 
\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\|f\|_2 \leq 
\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\|f\|_1.
</math>
Using [[Stirling's approximation|Stirling's formula]] applied to [[binomial coefficient]]s we get asymptotically a slight improvement when using binomial coefficients
:<math>
\|h\|_{\infty} \leq 
\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\|f\|_2 \approx
2^n\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi n}}\|f\|_2.
</math>

From the bounds on the individual coefficients one can deduce the following related bound.

If <math>f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]</math> is [[irreducible polynomial|reducible]] then it has a non-trivial factor <math>h</math> of degree <math>k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor</math> such that 
:<math>
\|h\|_{\infty} \leq 
\binom{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{\lfloor n/4\rfloor}\|f\|_2 \leq 
\binom{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{\lfloor n/4\rfloor}\|f\|_1.
</math>
Combining this with [[Stirling's approximation|Stirling's formula]] to replace the [[binomial coefficient]]s leads to more explicit versions.

While the upper bounds that are independent of <math>h</math> and only depend on <math>f</math> are of great theoretical interest and aesthetic appeal, in practical application one has usually information about the degree <math>k</math> of <math>h</math>. This is why the sharper bounds that additionally depend on <math>k</math> are often more relevant.

==Sharpness of bounds==

===Cyclotomic polynomials===

For <math>f=x^n-1</math> the [[cyclotomic polynomial]]s <math>h=\Phi_n(x)</math> is an [[Irreducible polynomial|irreducible]] divisor of degree <math>k=\varphi(n)</math>, [[Euler's totient function]]. In this case 
<math>\|f\|_{2}=\sqrt{2}</math> and it is custom to denote <math>\|h\|_{\infty}=A(n) </math>. A [[Cyclotomic polynomial#Integers appearing as coefficients|result]] of Vaughan states<ref name=Vaughan>{{cite journal |last=Vaughan |first=R. C. |date=1975 |title=Bounds for the coefficients of cyclotomic polynomials |journal=Michigan Math. J. |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=289–295 |doi=10.1307/mmj/1029001352 |doi-access=free }}</ref> for infinitely many positive integers <math>n</math>
:<math>\|h\|_{\infty} =A(n) > e^{\left(n^{(\log 2)/(\log\log n)}\right)},</math>
a superpolynomial bound in the degree <math>n</math>.

Comparing with Mignotte's bound and using [[Stirling's approximation|Stirling's formula]] as well as [[Euler's totient function#Growth rate|bounds for Euler's totient function]] we get for infinitely many <math>n</math>
:<math>
e^{\left(n^{(\log 2)/(\log\log n)}\right)}<
\|h\|_{\infty} \leq 
\binom{k}{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\|f\|_2 =
\binom{\varphi(n)}{\lfloor \varphi(n)/2\rfloor}\sqrt{2} \approx
2^{\varphi(n)}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi \varphi(n)}}\sqrt{2}\geq
2^{e^{-\gamma}n/(\log\log n)}\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi e^{-\gamma}n/(\log\log n)}}. 
</math>
This leaves a gap between Mignotte's upper bound and what is known to be attained through cyclotomic polynomials. Cyclotomic polynomials cannot close this gap by a [[Cyclotomic polynomial#Integers appearing as coefficients|result]] of [[Paul T. Bateman|Bateman]] that states<ref name=Bateman>{{cite journal |last=Bateman |first=Paul T. |title=On the Size of the Coefficients of the Cyclotomic Polynomial |date=1981 |journal=Séminaire de Théorie des Nombres de Bordeaux |pages=1–17 |jstor=44165422 |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/44165422}}</ref>
for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> for all sufficiently large positive integers <math>n</math> we have
:<math>\|h\|_{\infty} =A(n) < e^{\left(n^{(\log 2+\varepsilon)/(\log\log n)}\right)}.</math>
Also note that despite the superpolynomial growth of Vaughan's lower bound in practice looking at [[Cyclotomic polynomial#Examples|examples of cyclotomic polynomials]] the coefficients of <math>h=\Phi_n(x)</math> are far smaller than Mignotte's bound.

===A family of polynomials with exponential growth in the coefficients of its factors===

Abbot gives the following example<ref name=Abbot>{{cite journal |arxiv=0904.3057 |doi=10.1016/j.jsc.2012.09.004 |title=Bounds on factors in Z&#91;x&#93; |year=2013 |last1=Abbott |first1=John |journal=Journal of Symbolic Computation |volume=50 |pages=532–563 |s2cid=15176498 }}</ref> related to cyclotomic polynomials. Set 
:<math>
H(x)=(x+1)(x^2+x+1)=x^3+2x^2+2x+1, \ \ \ 
F(x)=H(x)\cdot H(-x)=-x^6+1
</math>
and consider for positive integers <math>j</math>
:<math>
h=h_j=H(x)^j, \ \ \ 
f=f_j=F(x)^j.
</math>
Note that the degrees are <math>k=3j</math> resp. <math>n=6j</math>. Abbot shows that asymptotically for large <math>j</math> we have
:<math>
\|h_j\|_{\infty}\geq 6^j\frac{1}{3j+1}, \ \ \ 
\|f_j\|_{\infty}\approx 2^j\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi j}}.
</math>
Using Mignotte's bound in the version
<math>
\|h\|_{\infty} \leq
2^{k}\sqrt{n+1}\|f\|_{\infty}
</math>
we compare
:<math>
3^{n/6}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3n}} \approx
\frac{6^j\frac{1}{3j+1}}{2^j\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi j}}} \lesssim
\frac{\|h\|_{\infty}}{\|f\|_{\infty}} \leq
2^{k}\sqrt{n+1}=
2^{n/2}\sqrt{n+1}
</math>
Ignoring the root terms leads to
:<math>
1.2009^n \approx
\sqrt[6]{3}^n \lesssim
\frac{\|h\|_{\infty}}{\|f\|_{\infty}} \lesssim
\sqrt{2}^n\approx 
1.4142^n.
</math>
Abbot claims that{{r|Abbot|p=24}} 
<blockquote>An exhaustive search in low degrees suggests that this family of factorizations is close to extremal.</blockquote>
While there is still an exponential gap between the example and Mignotte's bound, the example shows that exponential growth is the right order for such a general bound.

Note that Abbot also compares Mignotte's bound with other types of bounds and gives examples where Mignotte's bound is best and examples where other bounds are better{{r|Abbot|pp=7ff}}.

Also note that, while the cyclotomic polynomials <math>h=\Phi_n(x)</math> from the previous section are irreducible factors, the factors <math>h=h_j=H(x)^j=(x+1)^j(x^2+x+1)^j</math> have many factors themselves. Abbot speculates{{r|Abbot|p=32}} 
<blockquote>The examples [...] compel any ideal “irreducible single factor bound” to grow with degree, though the rate of growth appears to be much slower than for single factor bounds valid for any (suitably scaled) factorization in <math>\mathbb{C}[x]</math>. This suggests that such an ideal single factor bound could be very much smaller than the currently known ones.</blockquote>

==Generalizations==

Usually the Mignotte bounds are only stated for complex or integer polynomials. They are equally valid for any [[subring]] <math>R\subset\mathbb{C}</math>, in particular when considering only monic polynomials for which <math>\frac{|h_k|}{|f_n|}=1</math>.

Any abstract [[number field]] and its [[ring of integers]] can be considered a subring of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, however there can be multiple embeddings which are inequivalent with respect to absolute values. The Mignotte bounds are abstract and general enough that they hold independent of the chosen embedding. This may be taken as a hint that they are not as tight as possible in principle, as can indeed be seen from competing bounds that are sometimes better{{r|Abbot|pp=7ff}}.

==Applications==

In [[computer algebra]] when doing effective computations with integer polynomials often the following strategy is applied. One [[Good reduction|reduces a polynomial <math>f</math> modulo a suitable prime number <math>p</math>]] to get <math>f_p</math>, solves a related problem over <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> instead of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> which is often simpler, and finally uses [[Hensel lifting]] to transfer the result for <math>f_p</math> back to <math>f</math>.

Hensel lifting is an iterative process and it is in general not clear when to stop it. The Landau–Mignotte bounds can supply additional [[a priori]] information that makes it possible to give explicit bounds on how often Hensel lifting has to be iterated to recover the solution for <math>f</math> from a solution for <math>f_p</math>.

In particular this can be applied to [[Factorization of polynomials#Factoring univariate polynomials over the integers|factoring]] integer polynomials{{r|mathWorld}} or for computing the [[Polynomial greatest common divisor|gcd]] of integer polynomials{{r|vzG|p=166}}. Although [[Effective method|effective]], this approach may not be the most [[Algorithmic efficiency|efficient]], as can be seen in the case of [[Factorization of polynomials#Factoring univariate polynomials over the integers|factoring]].
